description: Team Nebula built an interactive Mars survival guide that uses NASA’s Perseverance data to help a simulated rover crew explore Jezero Crater, plan science stops, and save enough time and battery to return to base.
summary:
Nebula is an interactive Mars survival guide and mission planner that helps a simulated rover crew decide which science stops it can visit in Jezero Crater while keeping enough time and battery to return to base. The crew explores a map built with NASA Mars Trek imagery, inspects real Perseverance waypoints, and compares routes along the rover’s recorded path.
For each plan, Nebula estimates driving time and energy use, accounts for time spent at science stops, and checks the reserves left after the drive home. During a simulated drive, the crew can pause, propose another stop, and see whether it fits the remaining budget. By turning real NASA observations into mission decisions, Nebula lets students and analog mission teams practice balancing what they want to explore with what they need to get home.
details:
Nebula is an interactive Mars survival guide that lets users plan and simulate a crewed rover mission in Jezero Crater. Users explore a circular atlas built with NASA Mars Trek imagery, inspect real Perseverance waypoints, and choose science stops along the rover’s recorded path.

The route engine uses the recorded path and changes in elevation to estimate driving time and battery use. It accounts for time spent at each science stop and checks whether the crew can complete the round trip while keeping the required time and battery reserves. The interface shows terrain safety, time, and overall scores and explains why a plan passes or is blocked. During the simulated drive, users can pause, propose an extra stop, and check the revised return plan before committing.

Nebula makes the cost of a science detour visible before the crew commits. We hope students and analog mission teams can use it to practice deciding when an extra stop is worth the time and energy. Our next step is to validate the terrain estimates with higher-resolution elevation data and test the workflow in a field exercise.

We built the interface with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Leaflet, ran the route planner through a Node.js and TypeScript API, and used Python to prepare GeoJSON map layers. We deployed the app on Vercel so users can open it in a web browser.
